chunks: From him, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Ibn Muskhan, from Qutaybah, who said:

A man asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) while I was with him, saying: 'We send sheep with a Jew and a Christian, and a stray animal appears among them, so he slaughters it. Do we eat his slaughter?'

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Do not include its price in your wealth, and do not eat it, for it is merely by name (that they are called slaughterers), and one who can be trusted regarding it is only a Muslim.'

The man said to him: 'Allah the Exalted said: "This day all good things are made lawful for you, and the food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them."'
He (the Imam) said: 'My father used to say: "It is only the minor/insignificant ones (or: it refers only to specific cases) and similar to them."'

key_terms.الْعَارِضَةُ: A stray animal that joins a flock
key_terms.طَعَامُ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْكِتَابَ: Food of the People of the Book

ai.seo_question: Is the slaughter of Jews and Christians considered halal for Shia Muslims according to hadith?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that the permissibility of the 'food of the People of the Book' is restricted to their specific ritual slaughter (Dhabihah) rather than general consumption, a view supported by his father, Imam al-Baqir, who limited it to minor or specific cases. This distinction highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on the reliability of the slaughterer's intent and practice, distinguishing between the general Quranic allowance and the specific conditions required for the meat to be considered Halal.
